chapter_title: Concerning the Cross of Light: [...] trample upon it.
chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by later pastoral/institutional application (missions, alms collection, elect/catechumen practice) wrapped in a dialogue frame, with marked pastoral drift in the second half. The oldest recoverable teaching here is mainly a cosmological-soteriological kernel: the Living Soul/Cross of Light can undergo necessary distress for healing/liberation without reckoning it as sin (medical analogy), plus a (partly lacunose) mechanism linking destructive speech to demonic binding. One explicit Gospel citation is a later Christian overlay.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic dialogue frame (“Once again… questioned the apostle”) and explicit setting “in the congregation of the church”; functions as a framed rehearsal of praxis rather than impersonal cosmological exposition.
Institutional church logistics (superior/teacher, foreign brethren, alms, brought to the church) and anxious self-scrutiny; cosmos is used to regulate community practice.
Begins with hagiographic speech-attribution (“the apostle… says”), then resolves a practical case about obedience to superiors and travel for church work; application voice dominates.
Explicitly addresses “Every elect and righteous person” and legitimates walking for “work of God”; institutional category “elect” and paraenetic reward language mark later pastoral guidance.
General ethical contrast (lust/acquisition vs. sin/error) without systematic cosmological mapping; paraenetic extension of the walking rule.
Returns to teacher-sending and the disciple’s scruple; anchored in community obedience structure rather than impersonal cosmological mechanics.

paragraphs.core_text: Again, do not be afraid even with this; because the Living Soul is like this. As a person, if a disease will take hold of his limbs, and his heart [is sl]ow, his soul distressed, and he has pain in his disease. He seeks after a doctor to cure him, to make him strong of heart. And he cures, attends to, and gives him health [from] the disease that has risen up against him. So he thinks about this.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Begins the impersonal cosmological justification via a natural analogy (healing) rather than institutional rules; introduces the Living Soul as the subject of the mechanism (distress endured for cure/liberation).

paragraphs.core_text: [And] a wise person comes, knowing the formulas proper to a skilled doctor. If he shall achieve a healing of the one whom he [... ...] it, he recites over him the formulas that he knows, and he even tramples with his foot upon all his limbs! That person, who is ill, knows that this person is trampling upon him so that he might achieve a healing; rather, not doing this to him out of some enmity he had against him beforehand. Instead, all that he does, he does to him that he might make a healing of his body. And he expels [the] disease and the pain, trampling upon him to occasion this benefit. That person, who is ill, he can bear no anger nor hatred against this doctor, who tramples upon him. He can not hate him out of enmity, because he knows that he does this to him to his benefit.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Extended mechanism-analogy: necessary trampling/pain as therapeutic action; no church offices/alms/catechumen structure, and the logic is explanatory rather than prescriptive.

paragraphs.core_text: However, should someone come and trample upon him in enmity; he may hate, prevent and not permit him! For he knows that he tramples upon him in enmity; and as he strikes out of a wanton whim, he piles another illness upon his disease.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Completes the core distinction (healing-intent vs enmity-intent) needed for the later application; still within the explanatory analogy, not institutional practice.

paragraphs.core_text: Again, this too is the case with the Living Soul; whether in the earth, or in the Cross of Light. Should you walk along upon it on the path, should you trample the Cross, it may take no reckoning against you in anger nor wrath. For it knows that [you] walk upon it for relief and healing, to proclaim on its behalf. [You] walk because of it, to reveal its mysteries. Also, the distress of the bones, which you have oppressed, befits not sin, but is set towards the victory. Again, because of this nothing will be lost for you due to the distress of the bones and your toil; rather, it all accumulates to the relief (of the soul).
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the explicit Gospel/NT support citation: “As the saviour has said: ‘Where your heart is, your treasure also will come to be there.’” This entered the Kephalaia via the Gospel tradition (Mt. 6), so it is later Christian overlay rather than the oldest teaching substrate.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core cosmological mechanism (Living Soul in earth/Cross of Light does not reckon necessary trampling as wrath) is interrupted by a Gospel citation formula (“As the saviour has said…”), indicating later NT overlay grafted onto an older explanatory unit.
Returns to the institutional scenario (teacher/foreign brethren/alms) and reassures about speech; strongly application-driven and anchored to alms administration.

paragraphs.core_text: Rather, the word that wounds is this: should a person utter a saying for the sake of the murder of a person, or the murder of animals, or for [the sake of] the murder of trees and the Cross of Light, the lying word and the wrathful and the bitter, or a word of envy and [...] only, or a word of accusation, which someone will spread against his brother; this is the [wor]d that wounds [...]. Should the person utter it, it befits [si]n; because [he has br]ought forth from it the demons [...] concerning this [...] the righteous person, or [...] all of them, which I have proclaimed, in order that [...] his word to the fetter; because anyone who would [...] his word to the fetter. And again, he [...] his coming forth, they will bind him in the place wherein he has bound his [...].
paragraphs.temporal_note: Despite ethical exempla, the paragraph grounds guilt in a cosmological mechanism (demons brought forth; binding/fettering in a corresponding place), rather than in church discipline; no NT citation or institutional seam markers.
Applies the ‘word’ distinction directly to alms-speech and release/gathering; this is practical community regulation rather than the impersonal mechanism itself.

paragraphs.core_text: [He is li]ke this, a wise doctor who might turn back [... ...] his disease. As a wound is in his body, he cuts [...] this person who is ill, in his wisdom, [...] he [...] this wound, and he cuts it. After these things [...] and he places the soluble drugs upon it, so that [they will be able to diss]olve. He might incise it with the iron, and he casts it out [f]rom him, with the soluble drugs. And the wound is purified [fr]om the fever. After these events, he shall place the soothing drugs [...] and it heals up. That person, who is ill, he shall give [...] but he shall not [...] he [shall not] generate anger in his heart against him; because he knows that he is making the aspect of his benefit and his healing. After the cut that he may make, and the cauterizing that he may do there, he shall even give rewards to the doctor! He gives his thanks and is a friend to him his whole life through.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Continuation of the therapeutic-necessity logic in a detailed, explanatory register (incision/iron/drugs/cautery) without institutional offices; functions as core analogy supporting the cosmological claim about necessary distress for salvation.

Explicit institutional mapping of the analogy (elect, alms-giving, brought to the church; ‘purified in the image of the saints’)—cosmos is used to justify church feeding practice, so this is later pastoral application.
Directly about “the holy church that the apostle shall establish,” listing ascetic disciplines; institutional/paraenetic material characteristic of later church practice.
High application voice (“I command you, my brothers and my limbs”) and concrete eating/alms discipline with catechumen instruction; clearly institutional paraenesis.
Dialogue attribution and summative reassurance (“Then speaks the apostle… You have no sin therein.”) function as a formal closure beat, not substrate exposition.
Hagiographic reaction formula (rejoicing, thanks to ‘my master’) and generalized praise of persuasion; standard Kephalaia framing close.
